# Hydrology and crop water research notes

Access date for every source in this file: 14 November 2026. Every number below comes from a named published source or from arithmetic on the companion CSV files that I show in full. Anything I could not verify from a public source is labelled a GAP in plain words. Full verbatim links for sources whose links contain dash characters are recorded in the companion CSV files and in the report to the parent agent, because this notes file itself follows the rule of zero dash characters in prose.

## 1. The inflow series I could actually extract

* Series delivered: annual flow of the River Nile at Aswan, Egypt, gauge named in the source as Aswan, formerly spelled Assuan.
* Years covered: 1871 to 1970, one hundred years, no missing years.
* Source of the values: Cobb, G. W. (1978), The problem of the Nile: conditional solution to a change point problem, Biometrika volume 65, pages 243 to 251, Table 1 on page 249, as republished in Durbin, J. and Koopman, S. J. (2001), Time Series Analysis by State Space Methods, Oxford University Press, and distributed as the Nile data set in the R datasets package.
* File copy read for this work: University of Auckland Rdatasets text file at https://www.stat.auckland.ac.nz/~wild/data/Rdatasets/txt/datasets/Nile.txt and its documentation page at https://www.stat.auckland.ac.nz/~wild/data/Rdatasets/doc/datasets/Nile.html
* Unit as published: annual flow in units of ten to the power eight cubic metres. Conversion used: one published unit equals 0.1 billion cubic metres, so flow in billion cubic metres equals the published value divided by ten. Example: the published value for 1913 is 456, and 456 divided by ten equals 45.6 billion cubic metres.
* The source states there is an apparent change point near 1898. That warning matters and is quantified in section 3 below.
* What this series is not: the source does not state in the documentation I could read whether each annual value is a calendar year total or a water year total, and it does not publish a naturalisation method. I therefore treat it as gauged annual flow at Aswan as published, and I do not blend it with any naturalised series. The naturalised series published by later authors are reported separately in section 2 as summary statistics only, never mixed into the CSV.
* File: nile_inflow_aswan_series.csv with columns year, flow in billion cubic metres, flow as published, gauge, source. One gauge only. One source only.

## 2. Longer and later records that exist only as figures or summary statistics

These are real published records, but I could not extract a year by year table from any public copy, so none of their annual values are in my CSV. I report only the summary statistics each source itself prints.

* Hurst, H. E. and Phillips, P. (1933), The Nile Basin Volume 4 and later supplements, Government Press, Cairo, extended by later Nile Basin work. Shapland, Wheeler and Cascão (2025), The Nile Basin: Climate Change, Water and Future Cooperation, Chatham House research paper, Zenodo record 17748693, plot naturalised flows at Aswan from 1871 to 2015 for a water year running 1 July to 30 June and state: mean natural flow 91 billion cubic metres per year for measurements between 1870 and 2015; minimum 42 billion cubic metres in 1913; maximum 145 billion cubic metres in 1897. The annual values sit inside a figure only. GAP: the year by year table behind that figure is not publicly extractable in the copy I could reach.
* Wheeler, K. G. and coauthors (2020), Understanding and managing new risks on the Nile with the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, Nature Communications volume 11, article 5222, open copy at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7567800/ A naturalised reconstruction at Aswan from 1900 to 2018 gives annual flows between 45.6 and 120 billion cubic metres with a mean of 86.5 billion cubic metres per year. Method as stated in the paper: the period 1900 to 2002 uses a reconstruction from 41 gauge sites built by Deltares for the Nile Basin Initiative; flows from 2003 to 2018 use gauged flows at Dongola adjusted for estimated Sudanese use rising from 14.6 billion cubic metres in 2005 to 16.7 billion cubic metres in 2017. The annual values sit inside a figure and in a model that is not published as a table. GAP: no extractable annual table.
* Abdelazim Negm volume chapter by El Gamal and Zaki (2017), Egyptian Irrigation After the Aswan High Dam, in Irrigated Agriculture in Egypt, Springer, summarising the Aswan flood record: mean 110.4 billion cubic metres with standard deviation 17.4 for 1870 to 1871 through 1898 to 1899; mean 84.1 with standard deviation 13.8 for 1899 to 1900 through 1954 to 1955; mean 93.2 for the whole period 1870 to 1871 through 1954 to 1955. The chapter plots later annual supply downstream of Aswan from 1960 to 1961 through 2010 to 2011 as a figure only.
* MWRI (2000) as reported in Conway and coauthors, Egypt and the Nile Basin, Aquatic Sciences volume 67 (2005), pages 42 to 50: for 1871 to 1872 through 1998 to 1999 the average natural volume flowing at Aswan was 88.350 cubic kilometres per year, standard deviation 15.705 cubic kilometres per year, maximum about 142.378 cubic kilometres per year in 1878 to 1879, minimum about 45.879 cubic kilometres per year in 1913 to 1914. One cubic kilometre equals one billion cubic metres.
* Sutcliffe, J. V. and Parks, Y. P. (1999), The Hydrology of the Nile, IAHS Special Publication number 5: annual flow series are plotted from 1870 to 1997 for downstream sites including Dongola and Aswan, and the text states that Dongola records were extended back to 1870 using Kajnarty, Wadi Halfa and Aswan. The book itself is not publicly extractable as a data table. GAP.
* Why the summary means differ: 84.1 to 93.2 to 91 to 88.35 to 86.5 billion cubic metres across the sources above. The sources use different periods, different year definitions and different naturalisation choices. Anyone who averages these means together or splices the series together would be inventing a record. My frequency analysis therefore uses one series only, the Cobb series in the CSV, and uses the other sources only as a check on plausibility.

## 3. Frequency analysis computed from the CSV series

All arithmetic below is on the one hundred values in nile_inflow_aswan_series.csv. A reader with the CSV can reproduce every number.

Step 1, the long term mean. Sum of the one hundred annual flows equals 9193.5 billion cubic metres. Mean equals 9193.5 divided by 100 equals 91.935 billion cubic metres, reported as 91.94. Sample standard deviation equals 16.92 billion cubic metres. Median equals 89.35 billion cubic metres. Lowest single year: 1913 at 45.6 billion cubic metres. Highest single year: 1879 at 137.0 billion cubic metres.

Step 2, dry year definition. A dry year is a year with flow below 0.85 times the long term mean. Threshold equals 0.85 times 91.935 equals 78.14 billion cubic metres. Count of years below 78.14 equals 23. Share equals 23 divided by 100 equals 23 percent. Years below the median: 50 of 100, which is 50 percent by construction of a median with no tied values, reported because the task asked for it, and it carries no extra information beyond confirming the median split.

Step 3, dry years by decade. I use calendar decades, and the first and last rows are partial because the record starts in 1871 and ends in 1970.

* 1871 to 1879, nine years, mean 113.2, dry years 0, share 0 percent.
* 1880 to 1889, ten years, mean 100.9, dry years 0, share 0 percent.
* 1890 to 1899, ten years, mean 112.3, dry years 1, share 10 percent. The one dry year is 1899 at 77.4.
* 1900 to 1909, ten years, mean 85.6, dry years 3, share 30 percent.
* 1910 to 1919, ten years, mean 83.2, dry years 4, share 40 percent.
* 1920 to 1929, ten years, mean 82.8, dry years 3, share 30 percent.
* 1930 to 1939, ten years, mean 86.8, dry years 3, share 30 percent. One of the three, 1931 at 78.1, sits only 0.04 below the threshold of 78.14, so this count is sensitive to rounding in the published integers.
* 1940 to 1949, ten years, mean 81.5, dry years 3, share 30 percent.
* 1950 to 1959, ten years, mean 88.7, dry years 2, share 20 percent.
* 1960 to 1969, ten years, mean 88.2, dry years 3, share 30 percent.
* 1970 alone, one year, value 74.0, dry years 1.

Reading of the decade table: every dry year in this record falls in 1899 or later, and the dry share is zero in the first two decades and between 20 and 40 percent in every full decade from 1900 onward. That pattern is the change point near 1898 that the source itself flags.

Step 4, the change point split. Years 1871 to 1898, twenty eight years, mean 109.77, sample standard deviation 13.50. Years 1899 to 1970, seventy two years, mean 85.00, sample standard deviation 12.48. Years 1900 to 1970 alone give a mean of 85.10. The later regime mean of about 85 agrees well with the independent published means for similar later periods in section 2, namely 84.1 for 1899 to 1954 and 86.5 for the naturalised 1900 to 2018 reconstruction. The full record mean of 91.94 is pulled up by the early high regime and should not be used alone as the expected flow for a modern planning model.

Step 5, worst runs inside the extracted record.

* Longest runs of consecutive dry years, dry meaning below 78.14: two runs of length three. First, 1939 to 1941 with flows 77.1, 67.6 and 64.9, mean 69.9. Second, 1968 to 1970 with flows 71.8, 71.4 and 74.0, mean 72.4. The second run is cut off by the end of the record in 1970, so its true length in the real river is unknown from this series.
* Lowest three year window by mean flow, whether or not every year is dry: 1913 to 1915, flows 45.6, 82.4 and 70.2, mean 66.07, which is 0.719 times the long term mean.
* Lowest five year window: 1911 to 1915, mean 70.78, which is 0.770 times the long term mean.
* Lowest ten year window: 1919 to 1928, mean 80.07, which is 0.871 times the long term mean.
* Lowest twenty year window: 1912 to 1931, mean 81.73, which is 0.889 times the long term mean.

Step 6, the late 1970s to 1980s drought. This is a GAP in my extracted series and I will not soften it: the Cobb series ends in 1970, so it contains no year of that drought, and any dry share or run length I quoted for it from this CSV would be invented. What named sources publish about it, as summary statistics only, is this. El Sheikh and coauthors (2024), Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam can generate sustainable hydropower while minimizing downstream water deficit during prolonged droughts, Communications Earth and Environment, using the naturalised Aswan record from 1900 to 2002 built from Deltares work and the Dongola gauge: the ten years 1968 to 1977 averaged 88.4 billion cubic metres per year, the drought period 1978 to 1987 averaged 72.0 billion cubic metres per year, and 1988 to 2002 averaged 92.2 billion cubic metres per year. Wheeler and coauthors (2020), Supplementary Table 3, label 1978 to 1987 at 72.3 billion cubic metres per year as the dry hydrology used for the dam filling era. Hassan, F. A., Nile Floods and Political Disorder in Early Egypt, in the NATO ASI volume on Third Millennium BC Climate Change and Old World Collapse, reports a lowest flood discharge figure of 62 billion cubic metres for 1982 to 1984 and describes the 1987 panic as reservoir storage fell below 25 billion cubic metres. Those three statements are consistent with each other on the shape of the event, a decade averaging about 72, with the worst years near the low sixties, but none of them publishes the year by year table in a public copy I could extract.

## 4. Scenario probabilities and multipliers derived from the record

Two derivations are given. Both use the full one hundred year CSV record as the primary basis, because that is the series delivered. A sensitivity check on the later regime follows, because the change point makes the choice of reference period a real modelling decision, not a detail.

Derivation A, bands at the same multipliers the current model uses. Definitions: low band means flow below 0.85 times the mean; expected band means flow from 0.85 times the mean to 1.08 times the mean inclusive at the top; high band means flow above 1.08 times the mean. Mean equals 91.935, so the band edges are 78.14 and 99.29 billion cubic metres.

* Low band: 23 years. Probability equals 23 divided by 100 equals 0.23. Mean flow inside the band equals 71.77. Typical low year multiplier equals 71.77 divided by 91.935 equals 0.781.
* Expected band: 45 years. Probability equals 0.45. Mean flow inside the band equals 87.77. Multiplier equals 0.955.
* High band: 32 years. Probability equals 0.32. Mean flow inside the band equals 112.28. Multiplier equals 1.221.
* Check: 23 plus 45 plus 32 equals 100, and 0.23 plus 0.45 plus 0.32 equals 1.00.

The lesson in Derivation A: 0.85 and 1.08 are band edges, not typical values. A typical year inside the low band delivers about 0.78 of the mean, and a typical year inside the high band delivers about 1.22 of the mean. A model that sets its low budget at 0.85 of expected and its high budget at about 1.08 of expected is budgeting for the mildest year in each band, not the typical year in each band.

Derivation B, terciles of the historical distribution. Sort the one hundred flows from lowest to highest and split into the lowest 33 years, the middle 34 years and the highest 33 years. Tercile cut points by linear interpolation on the sorted values are 83.10 and 98.40 billion cubic metres.

* Low tercile: probability 0.33, mean flow 74.57, multiplier 74.57 divided by 91.935 equals 0.811, observed range in the tercile 45.6 to 82.4.
* Middle tercile: probability 0.34, mean flow 89.45, multiplier 0.973, observed range 83.1 to 98.4.
* High tercile: probability 0.33, mean flow 111.86, multiplier 1.217, observed range 98.6 to 137.0.

Sensitivity check on the later regime only, years 1899 to 1970, seventy two years, mean 85.00. Applying the same band edges as shares of that mean, 0.85 times 85.00 equals 72.25 and 1.08 times 85.00 equals 91.80, gives low band 10 years, probability 0.139, typical multiplier 0.788; expected band 43 years, probability 0.597, typical multiplier 0.966; high band 19 years, probability 0.264, typical multiplier 1.188. The typical multipliers barely move, all within 0.04 of the full record values, but the probabilities move a lot, because the later regime is less spread out around its own lower mean. Probability statements for this river are therefore statements about a chosen reference period, and the model must name its period when it names its probabilities.

What this means for the current model numbers, stated plainly. The current probabilities 0.25, 0.50 and 0.25 sit between Derivation A at 0.23, 0.45 and 0.32 and the later regime sensitivity at 0.139, 0.597 and 0.264, so they are not absurd, but they are judgment, and the record does not produce them exactly under either stated band definition. The current multipliers 0.85 and about 1.08 are band edges under Derivation A. If the three budgets are meant to be typical low, expected and typical high outcomes, the record supports multipliers near 0.78 to 0.81 for low and near 1.19 to 1.22 for high, with the expected budget at the mean by construction. Applied to the current expected Delta budget of 11.00 billion cubic metres purely as an illustration of scale, typical low would be 11.00 times 0.781 equals 8.59 under Derivation A or 11.00 times 0.811 equals 8.92 under Derivation B, and typical high would be 11.00 times 1.221 equals 13.43 or 11.00 times 1.217 equals 13.39. The current low budget of 9.35 and high budget of 11.90 are both closer to the centre than a typical low or high year in the record.

One more caution that the record forces. Annual flow at Aswan is not the same thing as water released for the Delta in a single year, because Lake Nasser stores about two years of mean flow and releases have in practice been held near the treaty share in most years, with cuts under the drought management policy in bad sequences. Single year flow probabilities therefore overstate single year supply risk and understate the real risk, which is a multi year run like 1978 to 1987 arriving on a reservoir already drawn down. A defensible model should drive its scenarios from multi year mean flows as well as single years. For reference, the lowest ten year mean in my extracted record is 0.871 of the long term mean, while the published 1978 to 1987 mean of about 72 against a naturalised mean of 86.5 for 1900 to 2018 is a ratio of about 0.83.

## 5. Egypt water budget anchors as officially published

Full rows, including links, are in egypt_water_budget_anchors.csv. Values below are recorded exactly as published, and where two official publications print different totals I record both and do not blend them.

* Nile share of Egypt under the 1959 Nile Waters Agreement: 55.5 billion cubic metres per year. Source: Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation, Strategy for the Development and Management of Water Resources until 2050, December 2016, which states the traditional resources include Egypt Nile allocation of 55.5 billion cubic metres per year due to the 1959 Egypt and Sudan agreement. The same figure is printed in Gabr (2022) and in every other official source I read. No disagreement found on this number.
* The full 1959 accounting, as printed in Nile Basin Initiative (2025), Reporting the Nile Basin: A Sourcebook for Journalists, Entebbe: mean annual flow of the Nile agreed as 84 billion cubic metres measured at Aswan; 55.5 allocated to Egypt; 18.5 allocated to Sudan; 10 counted as losses from seepage and evaporation. Arithmetic check: 55.5 plus 18.5 plus 10 equals 84. This 84 is an agreement assumption from the flow record available in 1959, not a current measured mean, and section 2 shows later published means ranging from 84.1 to 91 depending on period and method.
* Total fresh water resources, CAPMAS version: 59.68 billion cubic metres per year, built as Nile 55.50 plus deep groundwater 2.50 plus rains and floods 1.30 plus desalination 0.38. Source: CAPMAS, Egypt in Figures 2024, water balance table for Egypt, with the table itself naming the Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation as its source. The same total of 59.68 and the same four components are printed by the OECD (2025), Policies for the Future of Farming and Food in Egypt, citing Egypt Water Strategy 2050 and MWRI (2016). In one of the four years printed in the CAPMAS table, deep groundwater is shown as 2.10 and the total as 59.28.
* Total water resources, MWRI Strategy version: about 59.25 billion cubic metres per year, built in that document as Nile 55.5 plus deep groundwater 2.1 plus rainwater and flash floods 1.3 plus desalinated water 0.35. Source: MWRI Strategy until 2050, section on water resources, December 2016. The 0.43 gap between 59.68 and 59.25 is entirely explained by the groundwater and desalination components differing between the two publications. GAP of a different kind: no single official publication I found reconciles the two versions, so a model must cite which version it uses.
* Total water resources including reuse: 81.63 billion cubic metres for the most recent year printed in the CAPMAS Egypt in Figures 2024 table, against 85.50 to 86.66 in the earlier years printed in the same table. This total adds shallow groundwater in the Delta and reuse streams to the 59.68 of fresh resources. It is a supply accounting total that counts some water more than once as it is reused, and it must never be compared directly with the 55.5 treaty share as if they were the same kind of quantity.
* Agricultural use, share basis: agriculture accounts for 76 percent of total water use in Egypt. Source: OECD (2025) citing CAPMAS (2025), for the 2023 to 2024 year, with drinking water and other uses making up the rest. Egypt third Nationally Determined Contribution, November 2026, submitted to the UNFCCC, prints a similar picture, agriculture consuming about 76 percent, about 62 billion cubic metres, and the Nile supplying 55.5 billion cubic metres per year by treaty with total yearly available resources printed as 59.25. Note: the components printed in that NDC passage, 55.5 plus 2.5 plus 1.3 plus 0.4, sum to 59.7, not to the 59.25 total printed beside them. I record the passage as published and flag the arithmetic rather than correcting a source silently.
* Agricultural use, volume basis from the water balance used by Gabr (2022): measured gross irrigation Nile freshwater of 42 billion cubic metres per year, against a computed total net irrigation requirement of about 21 billion cubic metres per year, implying irrigation efficiency of 50 percent, with flood irrigation dominant. Sources cited inside Gabr for the balance: MWRI (2017), CAPMAS (2018) and Gabr (2020). This pair of numbers is the single most important anchor for the crop section below, because it says applied water in Egypt is on average about twice net crop need.
* Agricultural demand, press reported official figures: a Ministry presentation to the Egyptian Senate, reported by SceneNow in 2026, puts total annual water demand at 88.55 billion cubic metres, with agriculture at 68.1, drinking water at 12.45, industry at 5.5 and other uses at 2.5, against renewable resources printed in the same report as 65.35. I treat this as a press report of official figures, not as a primary publication, and its renewable total of 65.35 does not match either official total above, because it counts 7.9 of deep groundwater that the other publications count at 2.1 to 2.5. Do not use 65.35 alongside 59.68 in one budget.

## 6. Crop water requirements for Egyptian conditions

Full rows are in crop_water_requirements_egypt.csv. The file carries one row per crop per source per basis, because the sources do not agree and picking one number per crop without naming its basis would hide the disagreement. Conversion rules used, both stated in the task and in the sources: one feddan equals 0.42 hectares, so a value per feddan becomes a value per hectare when divided by 0.42; and one millimetre of water over one hectare equals ten cubic metres, so a value in millimetres becomes cubic metres per hectare when multiplied by ten.

Source one, the Delta standard. Gabr, Mohamed El Sayed (2022), Management of irrigation requirements using FAO CROPWAT 8.0 model: a case study of Egypt, Modeling Earth Systems and Environment, volume 8, pages 3127 to 3142, Springer. Weather data from 31 stations for 1985 to 2018. Table 6 is the Delta territory table. Values are net irrigation requirement, defined in the paper as crop evapotranspiration minus effective rain. Net irrigation requirement is not applied water. Delta values, in millimetres per season, with cubic metres per hectare in brackets: wheat net 127.2 (1272) and crop evapotranspiration 178.2 (1782); rice net 1144.1 (11441) and evapotranspiration 1144.1 (11441), with effective rain taken as zero; maize net 576.2 (5762) and evapotranspiration 576.2 (5762); sugar beet net 392.7 (3927) and evapotranspiration 419.2 (4192); potatoes net 244.8 (2448) and evapotranspiration 318.4 (3184).

Caution on the Gabr wheat row, stated unsoftened: the Delta wheat evapotranspiration of 178.2 millimetres is not credible next to the same paper own tables for other territories, which give wheat evapotranspiration of 226.1 in the Canal territory, 257.2 in Alexandria and 221.7 in Greater Cairo, and it is far below the west Delta CROPWAT result of 490.4 millimetres below. The Delta wheat crop coefficient printed in the table, 0.37, is also far below the coefficients printed for wheat in the other territory tables of the same paper. I record the row as published, I flag it here, and no model should use 1782 or 1272 cubic metres per hectare for Delta wheat without resolving this internal inconsistency. GAP: I found no erratum for this paper.

Source two, applied requirements from CAPMAS. Abdelwahab, Negm, Ramadan, Kuriqi and Abd Elaty (2024), Mitigating water shortages and enhancing food security through crop optimization: insights from the Eastern Nile Delta, Acta Scientiarum Polonorum Formatio Circumiectus volume 23 issue 4, pages 61 to 76, DOI 10.15576/ASP.FC/193864. Table 3 prints water requirements in cubic metres per feddan sourced from CAPMAS (2017), used for the Ismailia Canal area of the East Nile Delta. The paper does not state whether these are net or gross figures; they behave like applied requirements and I label them exactly as the paper labels them, water requirement, with the basis field in my CSV saying applied water requirement as published by CAPMAS. Values per feddan, with per hectare conversions in brackets: wheat, winter crop, 2153 (5126); rice, summer crop, 6972 (16600); maize, summer crop, 3908 (9305), and maize in the Nili season in the same table 3122 (7433); sugar beet, winter crop, spelled Sugar beat in the source table, 3959 (9426); potatoes, winter crop, 1713 (4079), and potatoes in the summer listing in the same table 2581 (6145).

Source three, MWRI duty tables. Sallam, Gehan A. H. and Abd El Nasser, Gamal (2006), paper at the Second International Conference on Water Resources and Arid Environment, Riyadh, National Water Research Center, Cairo. Table 1 prints crop water requirements in cubic metres per feddan from the water duty tables of the Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation (MWRI, 2003), by region. Lower Egypt is the Delta region. Values per feddan, with per hectare conversions in brackets: wheat in Lower Egypt 1464 (3486); rice in Lower Egypt 5521 (13145). The same table gives wheat in Upper Egypt 2008, Middle Egypt 1621 and Out Valley 1606, and rice in Middle Egypt 7085 and Out Valley 5548, which shows how strongly the duty depends on region. This table covers wheat, rice and cotton only. GAP: no maize, sugar beet or potatoes values exist in this source.

Source four, west Delta evapotranspiration check. Soil mapping study of newly reclaimed areas west of the Nile Delta, Australian Journal of Basic and Applied Sciences, volume 2 issue 1 (2008), pages 165 to 173, using CROPWAT 4.2 with the Penman Monteith method. Crop water requirements in millimetres per season: wheat 490.4 (4904 cubic metres per hectare); sugar beet 556.65 (about 5567); maize 668.5 (6685). No rice or potatoes values are printed in the parts of this paper I could read. These are evapotranspiration basis values for sandy newly reclaimed land west of the Delta, not for the old Delta clay lands, and I include them as a check, not as Delta values.

What the four sources together say, crop by crop.

* Wheat: published Egyptian values span 1272 net in the flagged Gabr Delta row, 3486 as an MWRI Lower Egypt duty, 4904 as west Delta evapotranspiration, and 5126 as a CAPMAS applied requirement. The current model value of 4200 cubic metres per hectare sits inside this published range, but it matches no single named source. If the model needs applied water for old Delta land, the two applied basis sources bracket it at 3486 to 5126.
* Rice: 11441 net from Gabr Delta, 13145 as an MWRI Lower Egypt duty, 16600 as a CAPMAS applied requirement. The model value of 12000 sits between the net figure and the two applied figures and matches none of them. Rice is the crop where the net to applied gap costs the most water, because flooding and percolation losses sit on top of evapotranspiration.
* Maize: 5762 net and evapotranspiration from Gabr Delta, 6685 as west Delta evapotranspiration, 9305 as a CAPMAS summer applied requirement, 7433 in the Nili season. The model value of 5800 is almost exactly the Gabr net figure. If the model treats its crop water numbers as applied water, maize is understated by roughly the full efficiency gap.
* Sugar beet: 3927 net and 4192 evapotranspiration from Gabr Delta, about 5567 as west Delta evapotranspiration, 9426 as a CAPMAS applied requirement. The model value of 5200 sits between evapotranspiration and applied figures and matches none. The CAPMAS figure is more than double the Gabr net figure, the widest disagreement ratio of the five crops, and I could not resolve which basis detail drives it. GAP: no third applied basis source for Delta sugar beet was found to arbitrate.
* Potatoes: 2448 net and 3184 evapotranspiration from Gabr Delta, 4079 as a CAPMAS winter applied requirement, 6145 as a CAPMAS summer applied requirement. Season matters more for potatoes than for any other crop here, a winter and summer crop are both grown in Egypt, and a single annual potatoes number is not defensible without naming the season. The model value of 4800 sits between the winter and summer applied figures and matches neither.

The governing point for the model: the model needs applied water, and the only Egypt wide efficiency anchor I found is the Gabr water balance pair, gross irrigation of 42 against net requirement of about 21, an efficiency of 50 percent. Dividing a net figure by 0.5 to estimate applied water is an assumption built on that one anchor, and it should be labelled as such wherever it is used, crop by crop, rather than treated as a measurement.

## 7. Yield response factors from FAO Paper 33

Full rows are in fao33_ky_values.csv. The original is Doorenbos, J. and Kassam, A. H. (1979), Yield Response to Water, FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper number 33, FAO, Rome. I did not read a publicly extractable copy of the 1979 original table itself. The values below come from two citable FAO secondary sources that both print the Paper 33 seasonal values as a table, and they agree with each other on every crop they both list.

Secondary source A: Allen, Pereira, Raes and Smith (1998), Crop Evapotranspiration, FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper number 56, Chapter 8, Table 24, titled Seasonal yield response functions from FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper number 33, at https://www.fao.org/4/X0490E/x0490e0e.htm The same chapter states that Paper 33 gives Ky values for only about 23 crops.

Secondary source B: Steduto, Hsiao, Fereres and Raes (2012), Crop Yield Response to Water, FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper number 66, Chapter 2 by Smith and Steduto, Table 1, titled Seasonal Ky values from FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper number 33, at https://www.fao.org/4/I2800e/i2800e02.pdf

Values, seasonal, dimensionless.

* Wheat: FAO Paper 33 does not give one wheat value. It gives winter wheat 1.05 and spring wheat 1.15 in both secondary tables. Egypt grows winter wheat, sown in autumn and harvested in spring, so 1.05 is the relevant entry for this model. A third FAO source, the FAO manual on irrigation with wastewater, Chapter 5, Table 19 sourced to FAO (1979), prints wheat sensitivity as spring 1.15 and winter 1.0, so the winter wheat value is printed as 1.0 in one FAO secondary source and 1.05 in two others. The model current value of 1.00 for wheat matches the wastewater manual printing and sits 0.05 below the Paper 56 and Paper 66 printing. Record the discrepancy, do not hide it.
* Rice: GAP. No seasonal rice value appears in Table 24 of Paper 56 or in Table 1 of Paper 66. The wastewater manual Table 19 gives rice water requirements of 350 to 700 millimetres and sensitivity described in words only as high, with no number. A Sri Lanka canal modelling paper on Scribd attributes stage values for paddy of 1.2 in the vegetative period and 2.4 in the flowering period to FAO Paper 33, but that is not a seasonal value and the host is not a citable publisher, so I do not deliver it as the FAO 33 seasonal Ky. The model current rice value of 1.20 therefore has no verification in any citable secondary source I could reach, and it may well be a stage value that was mistaken for a seasonal value at some point in its history. That possibility should be checked against the 1979 original before the number is used again.
* Maize: 1.25 in both secondary tables. The model current value of 1.25 is verified.
* Sugar beet: 1.0 in both secondary tables, spelled Sugarbeet. The model current value of 1.00 is verified. One nuance: the FAO manual on deficit irrigation practices prints a collation in which sugar beet appears with values 0.80 and 0.90 for different yield definitions, beet yield against sugar yield. The seasonal headline value in the two Paper 33 summary tables is 1.0, and the model should state which yield it is modelling if it ever moves away from 1.0.
* Potatoes: 1.1 in both secondary tables, listed as Potato. The model current value of 1.10 is verified.

Score for the model current Ky set: maize, sugar beet and potatoes verified exactly; wheat verified only after splitting by season, with winter wheat at 1.05 against the model 1.00; rice not verified at all.

## 8. Gap list, unsoftened

* GAP 1: No publicly extractable year by year Nile flow table exists for any year after 1970 in the sources I could reach. The records that run to 2015 and to 2018 exist as figures and as model inputs, not as published tables. Extending the CSV past 1970 requires the Deltares reconstruction or MWRI yearbooks, neither of which is public in extractable form.
* GAP 2: The late 1970s to 1980s drought, the most decision relevant event in the whole record for a storage based system, can only be described here through published period means of about 72 billion cubic metres per year for 1978 to 1987 and a reported worst figure of 62 for 1982 to 1984. Its year by year shape is not available.
* GAP 3: The extracted Cobb series does not state its year definition or its naturalisation status in the documentation I could read. It is gauged flow at Aswan as published, and it must not be relabelled as natural flow.
* GAP 4: Published long term means for Aswan flow range from 84.1 to 93.2 billion cubic metres depending on source, period and method, and no source I found reconciles them into one official series. Any single expected flow number is a choice among these, and the choice must be named.
* GAP 5: Official Egyptian water totals disagree with each other: 59.68 against 59.25 billion cubic metres for total fresh resources, with the difference sitting in the groundwater and desalination components, and one NDC passage whose printed components do not sum to its printed total.
* GAP 6: No applied water requirement for Delta conditions from a single consistent source covers all five crops. The applied basis numbers come from CAPMAS as republished in a 2024 journal paper and from MWRI duty tables from 2003 as republished in a 2006 conference paper. Both are second hand printings of official tables I could not read in their original form.
* GAP 7: The Gabr (2022) Delta wheat evapotranspiration and net requirement are internally inconsistent with the same paper other tables and with every other wheat source found, and no erratum exists. Delta wheat has no clean CROPWAT number from this work.
* GAP 8: Sugar beet applied requirement from CAPMAS, 9426 cubic metres per hectare, is more than double the Gabr Delta net figure of 3927, and no third source was found to arbitrate. The true applied figure for Delta sugar beet is unresolved within a very wide range.
* GAP 9: FAO Paper 33 seasonal Ky for rice could not be verified in any citable source. The model value of 1.20 for rice stands unverified.
* GAP 10: Egypt wide irrigation efficiency rests on one anchor pair, gross 42 against net about 21 billion cubic metres, giving 50 percent, as cited inside Gabr (2022) from MWRI (2017) and CAPMAS (2018). No crop specific or Delta specific efficiency series was found, so converting net crop need to applied water crop by crop carries an uncertainty that no source found here can narrow.
